verses.text: Then some Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and asked,
"Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat."
Jesus replied, "And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?
For God said, 'Honor your father and mother' and 'Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.'
But you say that if anyone says to his father or mother, 'Whatever you would have received from me is a gift devoted to God,'
he need not honor his father or mother with it. Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition.
You hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied correctly about you:
'These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.
They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.'"
Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, "Listen and understand.
A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it."
Then the disciples came to Him and said, "Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?"
But Jesus replied, "Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots.
Disregard them! They are blind guides. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit."
Peter said to Him, "Explain this parable to us."
"Do you still not understand?" Jesus asked.
"Do you not yet realize that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated?
But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these things defile a man.
For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.
These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him."
Leaving that place, Jesus withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon.
And a Canaanite woman from that region came to Him, crying out, "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon."
But Jesus did not answer a word. So His disciples came and urged Him, "Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us."
He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
The woman came and knelt before Him. "Lord, help me!" she said.
But Jesus replied, "It is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs."
"Yes, Lord," she said, "even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table."
"O woman," Jesus answered, "your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed from that very hour.
Moving on from there, Jesus went along the Sea of Galilee. Then He went up on a mountain and sat down.
Large crowds came to Him, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and laid them at His feet, and He healed them.
The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.

Then Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, "I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way."
The disciples replied, "Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?"
"How many loaves do you have?" Jesus asked. "Seven," they replied, "and a few small fish."
And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground.
Taking the seven loaves and the fish, He gave thanks and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
A total of four thousand men were fed, besides women and children.
After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Narrative — a confrontation over tradition, followed by teaching, a notable Gentile healing account, and a second feeding miracle.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers weighing the difference between man-made tradition and God's actual commands, and watching Jesus' mission visibly widen toward Gentiles.
context.mapLabel: GALILEE → TYRE AND SIDON → THE DECAPOLIS
context.setting: By the first century, Pharisaic oral tradition (later written in the Mishnah) had grown into an extensive code — ceremonial hand-washing before meals was part of this tradition, not something commanded in the Law of Moses itself, which is the core of Jesus' challenge in v.1-9.
context.custom: The "Corban" loophole (implied in v.5-6) allowed someone to declare money "devoted to God" and thereby legally withhold it from aging parents — a technically legal maneuver Jesus calls out as nullifying the actual command to honor one's father and mother.
context.timelineImmediate: Jesus deliberately travels into Gentile territory (Tyre and Sidon), where the Canaanite woman's faith becomes a turning point — a preview of the Gospel's eventual reach beyond Israel, well before the Great Commission formally opens that door in chapter 28.
context.timelineBible: This is the second feeding miracle in Matthew (compare chapter 14's feeding of the five thousand) — the seven baskets left over here, versus twelve after the earlier miracle, are often read as a subtle shift from a Jewish audience (twelve tribes) toward Gentile inclusion (seven, a number of completeness).

translation.meaning: Handed-down human custom — Jesus' argument throughout this section is that tradition had come to override, rather than support, God's actual commands.

To make common or ceremonially unclean — the dispute in this passage (v.1-9) is over the Pharisees' hand-washing tradition, never commanded in the Law of Moses, not the Levitical food laws. Jesus relocates the source of defilement from that external ritual to the internal condition of the heart.
A diminutive form — closer to "little dogs" or household pets than the harsher term for wild street dogs, softening (though not eliminating) the edge of the exchange.

occurrences.note: Used only in this one story — told twice, once in Matthew and once in Mark — and nowhere else in the New Testament.

translation.meaning: Jesus' assessment of the Canaanite woman's faith — the only time in Matthew's Gospel He describes anyone's faith this way.
The same visceral empathy word used before the first feeding miracle in chapter 14 — Matthew frames both feedings as acts of compassion, not just displays of power.

occurrences.note: Used only for Jesus Himself, or for a clear Christ-figure in three of His parables — the good Samaritan, the forgiving master, and the father of the prodigal son.

gospelParallels.note: Mark's fuller, more detailed parallel account of the tradition controversy and what defiles a person.
Mark's version of the Canaanite (there called Syrophoenician) woman's daughter.
Mark's parallel account of the feeding of the four thousand.

otBackground.note: The command to honor father and mother, and the penalty for cursing them — both quoted directly by Jesus in v.4.
"These people honor Me with their lips" — quoted directly by Jesus in v.8-9.
Elisha's earlier, smaller-scale bread multiplication — a precedent for the feeding of the four thousand.

context.sparkNotes: Jesus confronts the Pharisees for elevating tradition over God's actual commands, then a Canaanite woman's persistent faith earns her daughter's healing. "Dogs," the word Jesus uses in that exchange, appears only in this one story across the whole New Testament — and His rebuke of the Pharisees directly quotes Isaiah 29:13's "these people honor Me with their lips."

commentary.note: Henry is explicit that Jesus "doth not yet repeal the law of the distinction of meats (that was not done till Acts 10), but the tradition of the elders" — a mainstream 18th-century reading that lines up with the same distinction drawn in this chapter's own Translation notes: the dispute is about handwashing custom, not Levitical food law.

Barnes summarizes the whole passage in one clean line: "it is not the neglect of washing the body which defiles; it is the deep, inward corruption of the heart" — and lists evil thoughts first among the things that actually pollute a person, since thought precedes and produces every other named sin on Jesus' list.

On the Canaanite woman's reply, Ellicott offers a memorable reading: she "did not ask that the children might be deprived of any fragment of their portion; but taking her place, contentedly, among the dogs, she could still claim Him as her Master, and ask for the crumbs of His mercy."
